reading.rtitle: The Smart Guest: Let the Hotel Do the Work
paras: On a business trip, your time is the most expensive thing you have. Many travelers still spend the night before a big meeting ironing a shirt or looking for a pharmacy. Smart guests do something different: they have the hotel do it. Most business hotels offer laundry service, dry cleaning, and pressing, and they can have a suit pressed in about two hours. The secret is simple. Ask early, and ask for a time.

Problems in the room are part of travel, too. The room is too cold, the shower is weak, or the room next door is loud at one in the morning. Do not wait until check-out to talk about it. Call the front desk at once. A good hotel will have the thermostat checked by maintenance in minutes, or it will have someone speak to your noisy neighbors. If you need to sleep late, the do-not-disturb sign is your best friend.

Finally, check-out. Read your bill before you sign it. Incidentals, like the minibar or room service, are easy to forget and easy to get wrong. If something is not yours, say so calmly and ask to have it taken off. And if your train or flight is late in the day, have your bags stored at luggage storage. It is usually free, and it gives you one more free afternoon in the city.

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the guide?
choices: Business hotels are expensive, so smart guests do their own laundry and ironing in the room to save money for the trip.
Smart business travelers ask the hotel to do services and solve problems for them, early and calmly.
You should complain about everything at check-out.

bank.label: Say it naturally
items: I'd like to have my suit pressed before seven, please.
Could I get my blouse dry-cleaned by tomorrow?
The room is very cold. Could you have the thermostat checked?
I'm sorry to call so late, but the room next door is very loud.
Could I have my bags stored until five?
I didn't use the minibar. Could you take it off my bill?

listenings.text: Good evening, Ms. Ito. This is Claire from the front desk. I'm calling about your requests. First, we had the thermostat in your room checked by maintenance, and they repaired it, so the room should be warm in about twenty minutes. Second, your suit. We will have it pressed tonight, and it will be ready by seven a.m. We can bring it to your room, or you can pick it up at the front desk. And finally, you asked about the day of your check-out. No problem at all. We can have your bags stored until your train leaves. If you need anything else, please dial nine. Have a good night, and good luck at the fair tomorrow.

I have managed hotels for twenty years, and I can tell you what the perfect complaint sounds like. It has three steps. Step one: describe the problem in one sentence, without emotion. The room is cold, and the heating is not working. That's it. Step two: ask for one clear solution. Could you have someone check it, or could I change rooms? When guests ask for five things at once, we cannot help them fast. One problem, one solution. Step three: thank the person by name at the end. Thank you, Claire. It sounds small, but people remember it, and the next time you call, they will remember you. Angry guests usually get an apology. Calm guests usually get an upgrade.

extra_audio.text: First, I describe the problem in one calm sentence. Then, I say why it is important for me today. Next, I ask for one clear solution, like having the thermostat checked. After that, I confirm the time: by seven, or in ten minutes. Finally, I thank the person by name.
